title: The Plantation Club in St. Louis and the 'fight' that was Max Is Making Wax
summary: The gangster-run white club wants fast Limehouse Blues to cover fights, dislikes the bebop, and bouncers rush in when the band plays Max Is Making Wax.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Well, after those three days, we went into this club -- this is a big club in St. Louis. It was called the Plantation, the Club Plantation. It was a White club, and

they had dancing in there. The gangsters ran it, from what I understand. But they had a situation in there, we got our instructions from them when we went in that whenever a fight started in there, and they had three or four bouncers, always play... I think it was "Limehouse Blues" that they wanted us to play, and they wanted us to play it real fast. Either "Limehouse Blues" or "Sweet Georgia Brown" -- one of those pieces.

So when we're playing there, I guess about the third night... First of all, the people didn't particularly dig us, no way. Because the music we were playing they just couldn't dance to it at all. They'd had Jeter-Pillars there, who'd been playing this nice ballroom music, danceable and everything, and here we came in playing these Bebop Blueses and "Night In Tunisia" and things like that, Sarah singing in her respective style, because Billy.... You know, they liked him okay. but all in all, they weren't too happy with our band at all.

But one time, we were playing some number that had quite a few people on the floor dancing. Right after that number... Dizzy had written a tune called "Max Is Making Wax", and it was one of those way-up kind of things like something similar that... Dizzy made a thing later called "Things To Come." It was something similar to that kind of an arrangement. And

right after this nice thing that we had been playing, and we'd had a floor full of people, we finished that number and went right in to "Max Is Making Wax," which was a way up fast thing, and it wasn't possible to dance unless you was a really hip Savoy Ballroom dancer or something.

Anyway, we went into this piece and we were playing it, and all of a sudden the bouncers ran up -- "Where, where where is it?" "Where is what?" "Where's the fight?" "There's no fight." They thought we were playing a version of something along "Limehouse Blues," I guess.
